title: How far away are the stars?
new_ideas: a ladder of four rungs that the film climbs (each method a rung), returning at the end as the answer
a glass-plate flip-book that reveals the variable star (old plates animated as frames)
a coin on a far hilltop as the true size of Bessel's angle

lines.text: One night in October 1923, on a mountain above Los Angeles, a young astronomer took a photograph of a faint smudge of *light*.

plan.see: Night: a white dome on a wooded ridge, its slit open to a starry sky; far below, a scatter of city lights.
plan.beats: +0.0 rise: the ridge and dome come up from the bottom (1.6 s) | +1.8 the slit opens (blinds 0.8 s) | +3.0 tilt up along the telescope's line to a small oval smudge among the stars

lines.text: The next day, he looked at the glass plate, crossed out one letter in red ink… and wrote a new word, with an exclamation *mark*.

plan.see: A glass plate on a light box; a hand with a red pencil strikes out an 'N' and writes 'VAR!'; the real plate ★P-01 takes its place.
plan.beats: +0.0 slide: the plate onto a glowing light box (1.0 s) | +1.6 hand crosses out 'N' (quill, 0.8 s) | +3.2 writes 'VAR!' (note style, red) | +5.0 real-reveal ★P-01 (1.0 s)

lines.text: That one word moved a whole galaxy a million light-years *away*.

plan.see: Through the plate, the smudge becomes the Andromeda galaxy; it slides back and back into a vast dark page.
plan.beats: +0.0 iris into the plate (1.0 s) | +1.0 the smudge becomes the engraved spiral | +2.4 scale-out: it recedes geometrically (3 s)

lines.text: So how do you measure the distance to something you can never *reach*?

plan.see: A slowly turning starfield; nothing in it carries a label or a number.
plan.beats: +0.0 the sky turns slowly (camera rot 3°, 5 s) | +1.0 blinds: the stars shimmer into place

lines.text: A star is a dot of light. It has no size you can see, no edge, no *label*.

plan.see: Push to a single star: under any magnification it stays a point.
plan.beats: +0.0 push ×4 (3 s) | +1.6 an eyepiece ring inks around it: still a point

lines.text: A bright star might be close… or it might be huge and very far away. From here, they look exactly the *same*.

plan.see: Split: a candle close up and a lighthouse far off; both shrink to the same dot.
plan.beats: +0.0 slide in the two halves | +1.6 morph: each shrinks to an identical dot (1.6 s)

lines.text: For two thousand years, astronomers knew the stars must be far. How far, nobody could *say*.

plan.see: An old star chart unrolls; its constellations are figures and lines, with no distances anywhere.
plan.beats: +0.0 unroll: the chart (1.6 s) | +1.8 pan across figures (3 s)

lines.text: The answer came in four steps: a wobble, a blinking star, a red word on a glass plate… and a universe that would not keep *still*.

plan.see: A ladder of four rungs rises into the sky; on each rung, a small sign: a wobbling dot, a blinking star, 'VAR!', a fleeing galaxy.
plan.beats: +0.0 assemble: rungs appear one by one (0.9 s each) | +4.0 ride up the ladder

lines.text: Our first clue is a *wobble*.

plan.see: Clue tag 1/4; title 'Clue I · The Wobble'.
plan.beats: +0.0 clue tag 1 | +0.2 title

lines.text: Hold a finger in front of your face, and close one eye, then the other. Your finger jumps against the *background*.

plan.see: A drawn hand holds up a finger before a window; the finger jumps left and right as the two eyes blink in turn.
plan.beats: +0.0 wipe: hand and window (1.0 s) | +1.6 the finger jumps left/right twice (0.6 s each)

lines.text: That jump is called parallax. The nearer the finger, the bigger the *jump*.

plan.see: Two sight lines from two eyes cross at the finger; as the finger moves closer, the angle widens.
plan.beats: +0.0 grow: two sight lines (1.2 s) | +1.6 the finger comes closer; the angle opens (back)

lines.text: The idea is ancient. The Greeks looked for this kind of shift in the stars, found none, and some concluded the Earth could not be *moving*.

plan.see: A Greek observer on a flat roof under the stars, a measuring rod raised; nothing moves.
plan.beats: +0.0 unroll: the roof scene (1.4 s) | +1.6 the observer (Person, chiton) raises a rod | +3.4 stars hold still

lines.text: Now make your two eyes as far apart as they can possibly be: two sides of the Earth's path around the *Sun*.

plan.see: The two eyes become two Earths on opposite sides of a wide orbit around a gold Sun.
plan.beats: +0.0 scale-out (2.4 s) | +1.2 bloom: the Sun | +2.0 morph: eyes → two Earths labelled 'January' and 'July'

lines.text: Look at a nearby star in January, and again in July. It should shift, very slightly, against the stars far behind it. But does *it*?

plan.see: From each Earth, a sight line to a near star; it lands on two different points of the far background.
plan.beats: +0.0 the Earth rides around the orbit half a turn (3 s) | +1.0 sight lines grow | +3.2 the near star jumps against the background (small, clear)

lines.text: For centuries, astronomers looked. Why did they see *nothing*?

plan.see: A log book drops open; page after page records 'no shift'.
plan.beats: +0.0 drop: the log book (bounce) | +1.2 pages flip; each says 'no shift' (note style)

lines.text: The shift was there. It was just unbelievably *small*.

plan.see: Iris into the gap between two dots: the distance between them is a hair.
plan.beats: +0.0 iris to the two dots (1.2 s) | +1.6 a hairline arc between them

lines.text: In 1838, in Königsberg, Friedrich Bessel finally caught it, with a telescope built for one job: measuring tiny *angles*.

plan.see: The Königsberg observatory; inside, the split-lens heliometer on its mount; Bessel at the eyepiece; his real portrait pinned.
plan.beats: +0.0 unroll: the observatory (1.4 s) | +1.6 the heliometer inks on, its split lens visible | +3.2 Bessel (Person, look) | +4.6 ★P-05 cabinet card

lines.text: His heliometer split the image of the sky in two, so he could slide one star onto another and read the gap with great *precision*.

plan.see: Through the eyepiece: two half-images of the sky slide past each other until two stars touch.
plan.beats: +0.0 the view splits in two halves (wipe diag) | +1.4 one half slides until the stars meet (2 s) | +3.4 a fine scale reads the gap

lines.text: His target was a faint double star called 61 Cygni, which crawls across the sky faster than almost any *other*.

plan.see: In the eyepiece: a faint pair of stars; a dotted track shows it creeping across the background over years.
plan.beats: +0.0 Eyepiece with ★P-06 | +1.6 a dotted track grows behind the pair (trail)

lines.text: Night after night for more than a year, he compared it with two faint stars nearby that he believed were far, far *behind* it.

plan.see: Two faint companion stars are ringed in pencil; nights tick by in the margin.
plan.beats: +0.0 blinds: night after night (the sky strip repeats ×5) | +2.0 pencil rings the two reference stars

lines.text: A fast crawl meant it was probably close. But how *close*?

plan.see: A small note 'close?' in the margin.
plan.beats: +0.0 note 'close?' writes on

lines.text: Over a year, he measured its wobble: about a third of a second of *arc*.

plan.see: The real announcement page ★D-02; the number circled; a tiny ellipse drawn beside the star.
plan.beats: +0.0 a tiny ellipse traces around the star over a year (2 s) | +2.2 ★D-02 slides in; red circle round 0.3136″

lines.text: That is the width of a small coin… seen from thirteen kilometres *away*.

plan.see: A small coin on a far hilltop, seen from another hill across a wide valley.
plan.beats: +0.0 drop: a coin on a post (bounce) | +1.0 scale-out across the landscape (3 s) | +3.0 label '13 km'

lines.text: From that angle, Bessel worked out the distance: roughly ten light-years — a hundred million million *kilometres*.

plan.see: The gold figure '≈ 10 light-years' appears beside 61 Cygni.
plan.beats: +0.0 figure '≈ 10 light-years' (1.4 s)

lines.text: And it was one of the nearest stars in the *sky*.

plan.see: Pull back: 61 Cygni is a speck among countless others.
plan.beats: +0.0 scale-out ×20 (3 s) | +1.0 stars bloom around it

lines.text: Almost at the same time, others measured two more: Alpha Centauri from the Cape of Good Hope, and Vega from *Russia*.

plan.see: Whip between two more small eyepieces with their stars and their places pinned on a little globe.
plan.beats: +0.0 whip to Alpha Centauri (expo 0.6 s) | +1.6 whip to Vega | +3.0 both pinned

lines.text: But parallax only works for the closest stars. For almost everything else, the wobble is too small to *measure*.

plan.see: A ruler of light reaches out from the Sun to the nearby stars — and then simply ends, frayed, in the dark.
plan.beats: +0.0 a gold ruler grows outward (2 s) | +2.4 it frays and tears off at its end (tear 1.0 s)

lines.text: Clue two: stars that *blink*.

plan.see: Clue tag 2/4; title 'Clue II · Stars That Blink'.
plan.beats: +0.0 clue tag 2 | +0.2 title

lines.text: At Harvard College Observatory, around 1900, women were hired to examine thousands of photographs of the *sky*.

plan.see: A long room with tall windows; women at desks with light frames and magnifiers; stacks of glass plates; a real group photo ★P-02.
plan.beats: +0.0 unroll: the room (1.6 s) | +1.6 pan along the desks (4 s) | +4.0 ★P-02 pinned plate

lines.text: They measured, catalogued and compared stars, one plate at a *time*.

plan.see: Glass plates slide one after another onto a light frame; on each, tiny dots are ticked off.
plan.beats: +0.0 slide: plates enter and leave (stagger 0.5 s) | +1.6 ticks appear on dots

lines.text: One of them was Henrietta Swan Leavitt. Her task: find stars that changed in *brightness*.

plan.see: Leavitt at her desk with a magnifier over a plate; her real portrait as a cabinet card.
plan.beats: +0.0 iris to her desk (1.2 s) | +1.4 Leavitt (Person, 1900s dress) | +3.0 cabinet card from ★P-02

lines.text: Her plates came from Peru, where a Harvard telescope photographed the southern sky — including two misty patches called the Magellanic *Clouds*.

plan.see: A window to the Andes: a small observatory under a southern sky with two pale clouds of stars.
plan.beats: +0.0 window to Arequipa (1.2 s) | +1.4 crane up into the sky | +3.0 the two Clouds bloom; ★P-08 in an eyepiece

lines.text: In the Small Magellanic Cloud, she found stars that slowly swelled and faded, like a beating *heart*.

plan.see: Under her magnifier, several stars on a real plate ★P-03 pulse slowly — each with its own rhythm.
plan.beats: +0.0 Loupe over ★P-03 | +1.2 the stars pulse (breathe, different rates)

lines.text: She noticed something that no one had expected: the brighter stars beat more *slowly*.

plan.see: Two stars side by side: a bright one pulsing slowly, a dim one pulsing fast.
plan.beats: +0.0 two pulses (loops) | +1.6 labels 'bright · slow' / 'faint · fast'

lines.text: All those stars were in the same cloud, at about the same distance — so the difference in brightness was *real*.

plan.see: The pulsing stars gather into one cloud; a single distance line runs to them all.
plan.beats: +0.0 assemble: stars slide together (1.6 s) | +2.0 one dashed distance line

lines.text: In 1912, she published a graph of twenty-five of them. The longer the beat, the brighter the star — a straight *line*.

plan.see: Twenty-five points appear on a graph and fall along a straight line; the real circular page ★D-01 slides under it.
plan.beats: +0.0 quill plots 25 points (true to ★X-01, stagger 0.12 s) | +3.4 a straight line through them | +4.6 ★D-01 slides in; underline

lines.text: Her name was not on the title line. The director signed it, noting that it had been prepared by Miss *Leavitt*.

plan.see: The circular's heading; a small handwritten note 'prepared by Miss Leavitt' circled.
plan.beats: +0.0 drop: the circular's title area | +1.4 red circle round the line

lines.text: Time a star's beat, and you know how bright it really is. Compare that with how faint it looks… and you know how far away it *is*.

plan.see: A stopwatch times a pulse; its hand becomes a dial of true brightness; the dial becomes a long ruler stretching into space.
plan.beats: +0.0 a stopwatch times the beat | +2.4 morph: the hand → a brightness dial | +4.4 ride along a ruler into space

lines.text: Astronomers call these stars standard candles. Leavitt had given us a measuring tape for the *universe*.

plan.see: The ruler extends far beyond where parallax ended; at its tip, a small flame.
plan.beats: +0.0 the ruler passes the frayed parallax end (2 s) | +2.4 a small candle flame at its tip

lines.text: She never saw how far it would reach. She died in 1921 — two years before her stars changed the size of the *universe*.

plan.see: Her desk again, empty, the magnifier lying on a plate; the lamp dims.
plan.beats: +0.0 iris to the desk | +1.6 light-change: the lamp dims slowly (3 s)

lines.text: Clue three: one red *word*.

plan.see: Clue tag 3/4; title 'Clue III · One Red Word'.
plan.beats: +0.0 page-turn | +0.4 clue tag 3 | +0.6 title

lines.text: By 1920, astronomers were split over the faint spiral smudges in the sky. Were they inside our own galaxy… or were they galaxies of their *own*?

plan.see: A hall with two lecterns; two men in 1920 suits face each other; between them, a spiral smudge hangs in the air.
plan.beats: +0.0 slide: the hall (1.2 s) | +1.4 the two figures (Person) | +3.0 a spiral drawn between them | +4.6 ★P-09 two small plates

lines.text: In April 1920, two leading astronomers debated it in public in Washington. Neither could *prove* his case.

plan.see: The spiral between them tears in half.
plan.beats: +0.0 tear: the spiral splits (1.0 s) | +1.4 tremble

lines.text: The missing piece was a distance. And for that, you needed one of Leavitt's beating stars inside a spiral — and a telescope powerful enough to *see* it.

plan.see: The torn spiral mends; inside it, a tiny pulsing point appears.
plan.beats: +0.0 the halves rejoin | +1.4 iris: a tiny pulsing dot inside the spiral

lines.text: On Mount Wilson stood the largest telescope in the world, with a mirror two and a half metres across. But would even that be *enough*?

plan.see: Inside the dome: the giant open-tube telescope on its yoke mount, an observer's cage high on top; footage ★V-02 of a dome opening in an old screen.
plan.beats: +0.0 rise: the mount from the floor up (2 s) | +2.0 tilt up the tube to the cage | +3.6 ★V-02 in an OldScreen

lines.text: Edwin Hubble used it to photograph the great spiral in Andromeda, night after night, on glass *plates*.

plan.see: Hubble in the observer's cage, sliding a plate holder in; the spiral appears on the plate.
plan.beats: +0.0 Hubble (Person, 1920s coat, pipe) in the cage | +1.6 slide: a plate holder | +3.0 ride down the light into the plate

lines.text: Each exposure took a long time, with Hubble guiding the giant telescope by hand to keep every star a sharp *point*.

plan.see: Close on Hubble's hands at the guide controls, making tiny corrections; a cross-hair on a guide star.
plan.beats: +0.0 slide: hands on the controls | +1.2 Eyepiece with cross-hair: the guide star drifts and is nudged back (tremble small)

lines.text: But on one plate, he marked a new point of light as a nova — a star flaring up *once*.

plan.see: On the plate, a small 'N' is written beside a point.
plan.beats: +0.0 push into the plate | +1.0 quill writes 'N' (0.6 s)

lines.text: Then he checked older plates of the same spot. It wasn't a nova. It was getting brighter and fainter, again and *again*.

plan.see: Older plates flip by like a flip-book; the point brightens, fades, brightens.
plan.beats: +0.0 blinds: three plates side by side | +1.0 page-turn through them; the point pulses

lines.text: A beating star. One of Leavitt's *candles*.

plan.see: The pulsing point matches the heartbeat star from clue two, side by side.
plan.beats: +0.0 match: Leavitt's star slides in beside it; both pulse together

lines.src: S8 S10 S11 S5 S6 S7

lines.text: He crossed out the 'N', and wrote 'VAR!' — *variable*.

plan.see: The famous plate ★P-01, his red mark circled.
plan.beats: +0.0 ★P-01 real-reveal | +1.4 red circle round 'VAR!'

lines.text: Timing its beat told him how bright it really was. Its faintness told him how far: hundreds of thousands of light-years, far outside our own *galaxy*.

plan.see: Pull back from Andromeda past the edge of our own galaxy's disc, which shrinks to a small disc far away.
plan.beats: +0.0 scale-out across the gap (4 s) | +2.0 our galaxy's disc appears, small | +3.4 label 'our galaxy'

lines.text: Andromeda was not a cloud in our galaxy. It was a galaxy in its own right — and the universe was suddenly *enormous*.

plan.see: Two galaxies on one dark page; the space between them is vast.
plan.beats: +0.0 bloom: countless faint galaxies appear around them

lines.text: Clue four: a universe that will not keep *still*.

plan.see: Clue tag 4/4; title 'Clue IV · Runaway Galaxies'.
plan.beats: +0.0 clue tag 4 | +0.2 title

lines.text: Light from a galaxy can be spread into a rainbow. In most galaxies, the colours were shifted toward *red*.

plan.see: A spectrum strip with dark lines; the lines slide toward the red end.
plan.beats: +0.0 grow: the spectrum strip | +1.6 morph: dark lines slide red-ward (2 s)

lines.text: A red shift means the galaxy is moving away from us, the way a siren drops in pitch as it races *off*.

plan.see: An old ambulance drives away; behind it, the sound rings stretch out.
plan.beats: +0.0 slide: the vehicle drives off (3 s) | +1.0 ripples behind it stretch

lines.text: When Hubble set the distances from Leavitt's stars beside these speeds, a pattern leapt out: the farther a galaxy, the faster it was *fleeing*.

plan.see: Points plotted from the real 1929 table rise along a line; the real paper ★D-04 slides in.
plan.beats: +0.0 quill plots the points (true to ★X-02) | +3.0 a line through them | +4.4 ★D-04

lines.text: His first numbers were rough — his rate of expansion was several times too high — but the pattern itself was *real*.

plan.see: On the graph, Hubble's steep line is redrawn, much shallower, in modern ink — still a straight line.
plan.beats: +0.0 a second, shallower line is drawn over his (quill, 1.6 s) | +2.0 note 'still a straight line'

lines.text: A Belgian priest and physicist, Georges Lemaître, had already seen what it meant. The universe is *expanding*.

plan.see: A small window: Lemaître at a desk, his 1927 paper beside him.
plan.beats: +0.0 iris: the window (1.0 s) | +1.4 Lemaître (Person, collar) | +2.6 ★D-05

lines.text: Not galaxies flying through space — but space itself stretching, carrying the galaxies further *apart*.

plan.see: A grid of fine ink lines with galaxies on its crossings stretches evenly; every galaxy moves away from every other.
plan.beats: +0.0 grow: the grid with galaxies | +1.6 the grid stretches (4 s, linear)

lines.text: Think about what had *happened*.

plan.see: The ladder of four rungs returns, small.
plan.beats: +0.0 ink-on: the ladder

lines.text: People set out to measure how far away the stars are, and ended up discovering that the universe has a *history*.

plan.see: Ride up the ladder; at the top, the stretching grid; the camera keeps rising into the past.
plan.beats: +0.0 ride up the rungs (3 s) | +2.4 the grid shrinks backward

lines.text: If everything is moving apart now, then long ago, everything was closer together — all the way back to a *beginning*.

plan.see: The grid runs backward; galaxies crowd together toward a bright point.
plan.beats: +0.0 the stretch runs in reverse (3 s) | +2.6 all lines converge on a bright point

lines.text: And the same trick Bessel used for one star, a space telescope called Gaia now uses for more than a billion *stars*.

plan.see: A small spacecraft spins slowly; around it the sky fills with countless tiny ellipses — each a measured wobble.
plan.beats: +0.0 bloom: the craft | +1.6 tiny ellipses appear across the sky (particles, many) | +4.0 ★P-10 (if allowed)

lines.text: So — how far away are the *stars*?

plan.see: The starfield of the opening returns.
plan.beats: +0.0 iris: the starfield

lines.text: The nearest ones, a few light-years: close enough for a wobble to give them *away*.

plan.see: The tiny ellipse around 61 Cygni.
plan.beats: +0.0 the ellipse traces again

lines.text: Farther ones, by the beat of their brightest stars. And the galaxies — millions and billions of light-years away, still moving *apart*.

plan.see: Ride outward along the ladder of methods: the beating star, the red word, the stretching grid.
plan.beats: +0.0 ride outward (5 s) past each rung's sign

lines.src: S5 S6 S7 S8 S10 S11 S12 S13

lines.text: None of them ever left the *Earth*.

plan.see: Four small figures in a row at four eyepieces: Bessel, Leavitt with her magnifier, Hubble, and a modern astronomer at a screen.
plan.beats: +0.0 pan along the row; each inks on as passed (stagger 1.0 s)

lines.text: Every distance in the universe still rests on that ladder, and its first rung is still a tiny wobble, measured from *here*.

plan.see: The ladder rises from the row of figures into the sky; its lowest rung glows.
plan.beats: +0.0 grow: the ladder rises (2 s) | +2.4 the first rung glows gold

lines.text: They measured the universe from a desk, a dome and a pile of glass *plates*.

plan.see: The figures dissolve into a stack of glass plates on a desk, under a lamp.
plan.beats: +0.0 slide: the stack | +1.6 light-change: lamp warms

lines.text: Look up tonight. Some of that light left its star before anyone measured how far it had to *travel*.

plan.see: Tilt up from the desk through a window into the real night sky; the brand end card follows.
plan.beats: +0.0 tilt up through the window (3 s) | +2.0 the sky fills the frame | +4.0 end card
